title: Neurodiversity
text: The natural variation in how human minds work. The term describes diversity across people, rather than a diagnosis. A class includes many ways of thinking, learning, and communicating.

title: Neurodivergent
text: A broad, non-medical term for a person whose mental functioning differs from what is considered typical. People and communities use its boundaries differently. Someone with ADHD may describe themself as neurodivergent.

title: Neurotypical
text: A term for someone whose neurological development or functioning is considered typical in a particular context. It does not mean everyone in that group thinks alike. A neurotypical person still has individual learning and communication preferences.

title: Neurodiverse
text: Describes a group of people with different neurological characteristics. An individual is usually described as neurodivergent or neurotypical. A team with both neurotypical and neurodivergent members is neurodiverse.

title: Disability
text: A condition or difference that can limit activities or participation. Both individual needs and barriers in the environment affect someone’s experience of disability. A noisy testing room may create a barrier that a quiet space helps reduce.

title: Identity-first language
text: Language that places a disability or identity before the word “person.” Some people see this as recognizing an important part of who they are. “Autistic person” is identity-first language. Follow the individual’s preference.

title: Person-first language
text: Language that names the person before their disability. Some people prefer it as a way to emphasize their personhood. “Person with dyslexia” is person-first language. There is no single preference shared by everyone.

title: Neurodevelopmental conditions
text: Conditions that arise during development and can affect learning, communication, attention, or movement. Experiences and support needs vary widely. ADHD and autism are examples of neurodevelopmental conditions.

title: Hyperfocus
text: An intense period of attention on an activity, sometimes with difficulty switching attention to something else. Someone may become so absorbed in a project that they lose track of time.

title: Sensory sensitivity
text: Experiencing sensory input, such as sound, light, textures, or smells, differently or more intensely. Sensitivity can vary by sense and situation. A buzzing fluorescent light may make it difficult to concentrate.

title: Special interests
text: Deep or sustained interests in particular subjects. Many autistic people use this term for interests that bring enjoyment, knowledge, and connection. A person might enjoy learning extensively about transit maps or a favorite author.

title: Stimming
text: Repetitive movements, sounds, or actions that can help a person regulate sensory input, express emotion, or focus. Rocking, humming, or moving the hands may be forms of stimming.

title: Masking / camouflaging
text: Hiding or changing traits to fit social expectations. This can take effort and may leave a person feeling exhausted. Someone may rehearse conversations or force eye contact even when it is uncomfortable.

title: Restricted and repetitive behaviors
text: A broad clinical term that can include repeated movements, routines, and focused interests. Their purpose and impact differ between people. A familiar routine can help someone feel prepared for the day.

title: Visible and non-visible disabilities
text: Some differences are readily apparent; others are not. What you can observe does not reliably tell you how much support someone needs. A person may experience sensory overload without showing obvious signs of distress.

title: Accommodations
text: Changes to an environment or process that help a person participate and access the same opportunities. Written instructions, quieter spaces, or accessible learning materials may help.

title: Executive function
text: Mental processes used to plan, start tasks, organize information, manage time, and shift attention. A visual checklist can make a multi-step assignment easier to manage.

title: Sensory overload
text: Feeling overwhelmed when sensory input becomes difficult to process or manage. A crowded, noisy hallway may feel overwhelming; a quieter route can help.

title: Autism
text: Autism spectrum disorder · ASD Autism involves differences in communication, interaction, behavior, and sensory experiences. The spectrum describes varied combinations of traits and support needs. Offer clear expectations, respect communication preferences, and ask about sensory adjustments.

title: ADHD
text: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder ADHD involves ongoing patterns of inattention, hyperactivity, impulsivity, or a combination of these that affect daily life across situations. Break tasks into steps, make time and expectations visible, and offer movement breaks.

title: Dyslexia
text: A learning difference affecting reading Dyslexia can affect accurate or fluent word reading and spelling. Reading difficulty does not tell you a person’s intelligence. Offer accessible text, audio options, appropriate reading instruction, and time to process information.

title: Dyscalculia
text: A learning difference affecting mathematics Dyscalculia can affect understanding numbers, quantities, and arithmetic. Its effects can extend to everyday tasks involving time or measurement. Use concrete examples, visual aids, step-by-step instructions, and suitable calculation tools.

title: Dyspraxia
text: Movement and coordination differences Dyspraxia is commonly used to describe difficulties with movement and coordination, often in the context of developmental coordination disorder. Allow time, offer alternatives to handwriting, and adapt activities to individual needs.

title: Tourette syndrome
text: A neurodevelopmental tic disorder Tourette syndrome involves repeated movements and vocalizations called tics. Tics are not deliberate misbehavior and can change over time. Avoid drawing unnecessary attention to tics, allow breaks, and follow the person’s preferences.

title: OCD
text: Obsessive-compulsive disorder OCD involves recurring, unwanted thoughts, repetitive behaviors or mental acts, or both. Symptoms can cause substantial distress and disrupt everyday life. Take distress seriously and support access to qualified mental health care.

title: Bipolar disorder
text: A condition affecting mood and energy Bipolar disorder involves episodes of marked changes in mood, energy, and activity, including mania or hypomania and depression. These are more than ordinary daily mood changes. Avoid using “bipolar” as shorthand for changing moods; support access to care and flexibility.

title: Epilepsy
text: A neurological condition involving seizures Epilepsy involves a tendency to have recurrent seizures. Seizures can look very different between people and do not always involve convulsions. Learn the person’s seizure action plan and appropriate seizure first aid from a qualified source.
